questions.q: Which transport mechanism accounts for the gastrointestinal absorption of the vast majority of therapeutic drugs?
questions.explain: Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases that cross biological lipid bilayers down a concentration gradient via passive diffusion in their non-ionized, lipid-soluble form.

open.q: Name the primary mechanism by which most drugs cross gastrointestinal cell membranes during absorption.

questions.q: According to Fick's law of diffusion, which factor is inversely proportional to the rate of passive drug diffusion across a biological membrane?
questions.explain: Fick's law states that flux is directly proportional to concentration gradient, surface area, and lipid solubility, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness.

open.q: According to Fick's law of diffusion, which physical parameter of a membrane reduces the rate of passive drug diffusion when it increases?

questions.q: In which state does a weak acid or weak base diffuse most readily across lipid cell membranes?
questions.explain: Charged (ionized) molecules attract a hydration shell and cannot easily penetrate the hydrophobic lipid bilayer, whereas non-ionized molecules diffuse freely.

open.q: State the ionization and solubility state required for a weak electrolyte drug to passively diffuse across lipid cell membranes.

questions.q: A weakly acidic drug has a pKa of 3.5. In which environment will the greatest fraction of this drug exist in its non-ionized, absorbable form?
questions.explain: By the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, weak acids remain predominantly protonated (non-ionized, HA) when the surrounding pH is lower than their pKa.

open.q: Explain whether a weakly acidic drug with a pKa of 3.5 is predominantly ionized or non-ionized in acidic gastric juice at pH 1.5.

questions.q: What happens to a weakly basic drug (pKa 8.5) after it is absorbed from the small intestine into the acidic gastric lumen (pH 1.5)?
options: It becomes protonated and trapped in the stomach as a water-soluble cation
It becomes completely non-ionized and diffuses back into plasma
It precipitates as an insoluble calcium salt
It undergoes immediate hepatic glucuronidation in the gastric wall
questions.explain: This phenomenon is ion trapping: weak bases accept protons in acidic gastric juice (BH+), becoming ionized and unable to diffuse back across the gastric mucosa.

open.q: Name the pharmacokinetic phenomenon whereby a weak base accumulates in an acidic compartment because it becomes ionized and cannot diffuse back across the membrane.

questions.q: Why are most orally administered weak acids (such as aspirin) still absorbed predominantly in the small intestine rather than the stomach despite being more non-ionized in gastric acid?
options: The stomach has no blood supply
The small intestine has extensive villi, microvilli and blood flow
Aspirin is absorbed only by ileal pumps
Gastric mucus blocks all passive diffusion
questions.explain: Although the non-ionized fraction is higher in the stomach, the huge surface area of the small intestinal villi and microvilli plus rich splanchnic perfusion make the small intestine the primary site of absorption.

open.q: Give the main anatomical reason why weakly acidic drugs are absorbed mainly in the small intestine rather than the stomach.
accept: enormous surface area of villi and microvilli
much larger absorptive surface area in the small intestine

questions.q: Which efflux transporter expressed on the apical membrane of intestinal enterocytes pumps many absorbed drugs back into the gut lumen, reducing oral bioavailability?
questions.explain: P-glycoprotein (MDR1/ABCB1) is an ATP-dependent efflux pump in enterocytes, hepatocytes, renal tubules, and the blood-brain barrier that limits drug entry.

open.q: Name the ATP-dependent efflux transporter in intestinal enterocytes and the blood-brain barrier that pumps drugs out of cells.

questions.q: How is the oral bioavailability (F) of a drug mathematically defined?
options: Plasma volume cleared of drug per unit time
Fraction of dose reaching systemic blood unchanged
questions.explain: Bioavailability (F) is calculated as (AUC oral / AUC IV) x 100% for equal doses, representing the fraction of unchanged drug entering systemic circulation.

open.q: Define bioavailability.
accept: fraction of administered dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged
percentage of drug dose entering systemic blood in unchanged form

questions.q: Which pharmacokinetic parameter obtained from a plasma concentration-time curve is directly used to calculate the extent of systemic drug absorption (bioavailability)?
options: Area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC)
questions.explain: AUC reflects the total systemic exposure to a drug over time; comparing AUC after extravascular dosing to AUC after intravenous dosing yields absolute bioavailability.

open.q: Which parameter derived from a plasma drug concentration-time plot measures total systemic drug exposure and is used to calculate bioavailability?

questions.q: A 200 mg oral dose of a drug produces an AUC of 40 mg·h/L, whereas a 100 mg intravenous dose of the same drug produces an AUC of 80 mg·h/L. What is the absolute oral bioavailability (F) of this drug?

open.q: Calculate the absolute oral bioavailability if a 200 mg oral dose yields an AUC of 40 mg·h/L and a 100 mg IV dose yields an AUC of 80 mg·h/L.

questions.q: What is meant by bioequivalence between two pharmaceutical formulations containing the same active ingredient?
options: They are made by the same manufacturer
They have identical appearance and excipients
They show similar Cmax, Tmax and AUC
questions.explain: Two drug products are bioequivalent if their bioavailability (rate and extent of systemic absorption) falls within accepted regulatory limits (typically 80% to 125% for 90% CI of AUC and Cmax).

open.q: Define bioequivalence between two formulations of the same drug.
accept: comparable rate and extent of absorption
no significant difference in bioavailability Cmax Tmax and AUC

questions.q: Why does co-administration of oral tetracycline with milk or aluminium-magnesium antacids markedly reduce tetracycline absorption?
options: Tetracycline is destroyed by alkaline pH
Tetracycline chelates calcium, magnesium and aluminium
questions.explain: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones chelate polyvalent metal cations in the GI lumen to form non-absorbable complexes.

open.q: Explain the mechanism by which milk or antacids decrease the oral absorption of tetracycline.
accept: chelation with divalent and trivalent cations
formation of insoluble complexes with calcium magnesium or aluminium

questions.q: What is the first-pass (presystemic) effect?
options: Metabolism of an orally absorbed drug in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation
Immediate renal excretion of a drug during its first pass through the glomerulus
Initial binding of a drug to red blood cells in the pulmonary capillaries
Destruction of an intravenous drug by plasma esterases within one second
questions.explain: Drugs absorbed from the GI tract enter the portal venous system and pass through the liver before entering the inferior vena cava, where high hepatic extraction reduces systemic bioavailability.

open.q: Define first-pass metabolism.
accept: presystemic metabolism in gut wall and liver before reaching systemic circulation
hepatic extraction of orally absorbed drug prior to systemic entry

questions.q: Which of the following drugs undergoes such extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism that oral administration is completely ineffective and it must be given parenterally?
questions.explain: Lidocaine undergoes nearly complete first-pass hepatic de-ethylation when taken orally (forming toxic metabolites without antiarrhythmic efficacy), so it is administered IV or locally.

open.q: Name a commonly used local anesthetic and class Ib antiarrhythmic drug that cannot be given orally due to nearly 100% hepatic first-pass metabolism.

questions.q: Which plasma protein is the primary binding site for acidic drugs such as warfarin, phenytoin, and salicylates?
questions.explain: Human serum albumin binds predominantly acidic and neutral drugs, whereas alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (orosomucoid) binds basic drugs such as lidocaine, propranolol, and quinidine.

open.q: Name the main plasma protein that binds weakly acidic drugs in the bloodstream.

questions.q: Which acute-phase plasma protein primarily binds basic drugs such as lidocaine, propranolol, and imipramine?
questions.explain: Alpha-1-acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs and increases during acute inflammation, trauma, or myocardial infarction, altering free drug fractions.

open.q: Identify the plasma protein that preferentially binds basic drugs.

questions.q: Which fraction of a drug in plasma is pharmacologically active and capable of diffusing across capillary membranes to reach receptor sites and undergo glomerular filtration?
questions.explain: Protein-bound drug is too large to cross capillary endothelium or glomerular membranes and acts as an inactive circulating reservoir; only unbound drug is active.

open.q: Which fraction of a drug in plasma is pharmacologically active and available for tissue distribution and glomerular filtration?

questions.q: How is the apparent volume of distribution (Vd) defined?
options: Actual anatomical volume of the liver and kidneys combined
Total amount of drug in the body divided by the plasma drug concentration
Volume of urine excreted per minute multiplied by plasma concentration
Total plasma volume minus interstitial fluid volume
questions.explain: Vd = Amount of drug in body / Plasma concentration (C0). It is an apparent theoretical volume indicating the extent of extravascular tissue sequestration.

open.q: State the formula or definition of apparent volume of distribution (Vd).
accept: amount of drug in the body divided by plasma concentration

questions.q: A 70 kg patient receives an intravenous bolus of 500 mg of a drug, and the extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero (C0) is 10 mg/L. What is the apparent volume of distribution (Vd)?
questions.explain: Vd = Dose / C0 = 500 mg / 10 mg/L = 50 L, indicating distribution beyond plasma into total body water and tissues.

open.q: Calculate the apparent volume of distribution when a 500 mg IV bolus produces an initial plasma concentration of 10 mg/L.

questions.q: Chloroquine has an apparent volume of distribution of approximately 15,000 L in a 70 kg adult. What does this exceptionally large Vd indicate?
options: Chloroquine is confined strictly to the intravascular plasma compartment
Chloroquine is immediately excreted unchanged in exhaled air
Chloroquine binds 100% irreversibly to plasma albumin
Chloroquine is extensively concentrated and sequestered inside extravascular tissues
questions.explain: A Vd far exceeding total body water (~42 L) means plasma concentration is kept very low because the drug accumulates heavily in tissues (such as liver, retina, and melanin-containing cells).

open.q: What does an apparent volume of distribution much greater than total body water (e.g., 15,000 L for chloroquine) signify?

questions.q: Why does an intravenous bolus of thiopental sodium produce general anesthesia within 15 to 20 seconds, yet the patient awakens within 5 to 10 minutes even though the drug's elimination half-life is over 10 hours?
options: Thiopental rapidly redistributes from brain to muscle and fat
The kidneys clear it unchanged within five minutes
questions.explain: Thiopental is highly lipophilic and enters the richly perfused brain immediately, but its action terminates rapidly due to redistribution into less well-perfused muscle and fat stores.

open.q: Name the pharmacokinetic process responsible for the rapid termination of anesthesia after a single IV bolus of thiopental.

questions.q: Which structural feature of cerebral capillaries restricts the entry of polar, water-soluble drugs across the blood-brain barrier?
options: Tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells, supported by astrocyte end-feet
questions.explain: Cerebral capillary endothelial cells lack fenestrations, are sealed by tight junctions, are enveloped by glial foot processes, and express efflux transporters like P-glycoprotein.

open.q: Describe the key anatomical feature of brain capillaries that forms the blood-brain barrier.
accept: tight junctions between non-fenestrated endothelial cells
continuous endothelium with tight junctions and astrocyte foot processes

questions.q: A patient with acute bacterial meningitis is treated with intravenous benzylpenicillin, which normally penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly. Why does benzylpenicillin achieve therapeutic CSF concentrations in this patient?
options: Bacteria actively transport penicillin into neurons
Fever converts penicillin into a lipid-soluble ester
questions.explain: Inflammation of the meninges increases capillary permeability and opens tight junctions, allowing hydrophilic antibiotics like penicillin G to reach therapeutic levels in CSF.

open.q: Explain why hydrophilic antibiotics such as benzylpenicillin penetrate the CSF better during acute meningitis than in healthy individuals.
accept: meningeal inflammation increases blood-brain barrier permeability

questions.q: Why is levodopa administered rather than dopamine itself to treat Parkinson's disease?
options: Dopamine is destroyed by gastric acid
Levodopa crosses the BBB via an amino-acid transporter and is converted to dopamine
questions.explain: Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; its precursor levodopa enters the CNS via the LAT1 neutral amino acid carrier and is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase.

open.q: Explain why levodopa is used instead of dopamine to replenish central dopamine in Parkinson's disease.
accept: dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier while levodopa crosses via amino acid transport
levodopa crosses the BBB and is converted to dopamine

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes drug transfer across the human placenta?
options: Lipophilic, non-ionized drugs of low molecular weight cross the placenta readily by passive diffusion
The placenta is an absolute barrier that blocks all maternal medications
Only drugs with molecular weight above 10,000 Daltons cross the placenta
All drugs cross the placenta exclusively by active ATP-dependent pumps
questions.explain: The placenta is a lipid membrane; non-ionized lipophilic drugs cross easily by passive diffusion, whereas large macromolecules like heparin and insulin do not cross.

open.q: What types of drugs cross the placental barrier most readily?
accept: lipophilic non-ionized low molecular weight drugs

questions.q: A pregnant woman with deep vein thrombosis requires anticoagulation. Why is unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin preferred over warfarin during the first trimester and near term?
options: Heparin does not cross placenta; warfarin can harm the fetus
questions.explain: Heparin's high molecular weight and negative charge prevent placental transfer, avoiding fetal warfarin syndrome (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) and fetal hemorrhage.

open.q: Explain on a pharmacokinetic basis why heparin is safe for the fetus during pregnancy compared with warfarin.
accept: heparin does not cross the placenta due to large size and negative charge
heparin cannot cross the placental barrier

questions.q: A premature neonate develops unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and is inadvertently given sulfisoxazole (a sulfonamide). Soon after, the infant develops kernicterus. What is the pharmacokinetic mechanism?
options: It displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin, increasing free bilirubin
It causes haemolysis in every neonate
questions.explain: Sulfonamides compete with bilirubin for albumin binding; displaced free bilirubin crosses the immature neonatal blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia (kernicterus).

open.q: Explain the drug-binding interaction by which sulfonamides precipitate kernicterus in jaundiced neonates.
accept: displacement of bilirubin from plasma albumin
competes with bilirubin for albumin binding sites

questions.q: What is the primary chemical objective of drug biotransformation (metabolism) in the body?
options: Make water-soluble drugs lipid-soluble for storage
Make lipophilic drugs more polar for renal or biliary excretion
questions.explain: Lipophilic drugs are filtered at the glomerulus but passively reabsorbed across renal tubular cells; biotransformation adds or exposes polar groups so metabolites can be excreted.

open.q: State the main physiological purpose of hepatic drug metabolism.
accept: convert lipid-soluble drugs into water-soluble polar metabolites for excretion
increase polarity and water solubility for elimination

questions.q: Which types of chemical reactions constitute Phase I drug biotransformation?
options: Methylation, glutathione conjugation, and glycine conjugation
questions.explain: Phase I (functionalization) reactions introduce or unmask a polar functional group (-OH, -NH2, -SH, -COOH) via oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis.

open.q: Name the three main types of chemical reactions involved in Phase I drug metabolism.

questions.q: Where within the hepatocyte are the cytochrome P450 (CYP) monooxygenase enzymes predominantly located?
questions.explain: Cytochrome P450 enzymes and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases are membrane-bound enzymes embedded in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, isolated experimentally as microsomes.

open.q: Identify the subcellular organelle in hepatocytes where cytochrome P450 enzymes are located.

questions.q: Which cytochrome P450 isoenzyme is responsible for metabolizing the largest proportion (roughly 50%) of clinically used drugs?
questions.explain: CYP3A4, abundant in both liver and intestinal enterocytes, metabolizes approximately half of all marketed drugs, including calcium channel blockers, statins, and macrolides.

open.q: Name the single most abundant cytochrome P450 enzyme in human liver and intestine responsible for metabolizing about half of clinical drugs.

questions.q: Which cofactor is required by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases along with molecular oxygen to oxidize drugs?
questions.explain: Cytochrome P450 reductase transfers electrons from NADPH to the haem iron of cytochrome P450, activating molecular oxygen to incorporate one oxygen atom into the drug and reduce the other to water.

open.q: Name the reduced pyridine nucleotide cofactor required by the cytochrome P450 enzyme system.

questions.q: Which Phase II conjugation reaction is the ONLY one catalyzed by microsomal enzymes in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum rather than cytosolic enzymes?
questions.explain: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) are located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and can therefore be induced by microsomal enzyme inducers like phenobarbital and rifampicin.

open.q: Which Phase II conjugation pathway is catalyzed by microsomal enzymes in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?

questions.q: What is the activated endogenous donor molecule required for glucuronidation reactions?
questions.explain: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase transfers glucuronic acid from UDPGA to hydroxyl, carboxyl, amino, or thiol groups on drugs and bilirubin.

open.q: Name the high-energy donor molecule that supplies glucuronic acid during Phase II glucuronidation.

questions.q: A newborn infant treated with chloramphenicol develops abdominal distension, vomiting, progressive cyanosis, and vasomotor collapse ('grey baby syndrome'). Which immature hepatic enzyme pathway underlies this toxicity?
questions.explain: Neonates have deficient hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity and immature renal clearance, leading to accumulation of unconjugated chloramphenicol that inhibits mitochondrial electron transport.

open.q: Which hepatic enzyme deficiency in neonates causes grey baby syndrome upon exposure to chloramphenicol?

questions.q: Which genetic polymorphism in Phase II drug metabolism predisposes patients taking isoniazid to peripheral neuropathy (in slow metabolizers) or drug-induced hepatitis (in rapid metabolizers)?
questions.explain: Slow acetylators accumulate parent isoniazid, risking pyridoxine-deficiency peripheral neuropathy and drug-induced lupus; rapid acetylators generate more acetylhydrazine hepatotoxic intermediates.

open.q: Name the Phase II metabolic polymorphism that divides patients into slow and rapid metabolizers of isoniazid, hydralazine, and procainamide.

questions.q: Which of the following is a potent cytochrome P450 enzyme inducer capable of accelerating the metabolism of oral contraceptives and warfarin?
questions.explain: Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and St John's wort induce CYP enzymes, reducing plasma concentrations of co-administered drugs like warfarin and oral contraceptives.

open.q: Name a first-line antituberculosis drug that is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes.

questions.q: Which of the following substances inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 when consumed with oral felodipine or simvastatin, leading to markedly elevated plasma drug levels and toxicity?
questions.explain: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit juice cause mechanism-based (irreversible) inhibition of intestinal CYP3A4, increasing oral bioavailability of CYP3A4 substrates.

open.q: Name the dietary fruit product that irreversibly inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and increases the bioavailability of calcium channel blockers and statins.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman stabilized on combined oral contraceptive pills is started on rifampicin and isoniazid for pulmonary tuberculosis. Two months later she becomes pregnant despite strict pill adherence. What caused contraceptive failure?
options: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4, increasing contraceptive hormone clearance
questions.explain: Rifampicin strongly induces hepatic CYP3A4, lowering circulating steroid hormone levels below the threshold required to suppress ovulation.

open.q: Explain the pharmacokinetic interaction responsible for oral contraceptive failure in a patient started on rifampicin.
accept: CYP3A4 enzyme induction accelerating contraceptive metabolism

questions.q: A patient stabilized on warfarin is prescribed ketoconazole for a systemic fungal infection and subsequently presents with epistaxis and an INR of 7.2. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Ketoconazole converts warfarin into a thrombolytic
Ketoconazole inhibits CYP enzymes, reducing warfarin clearance
questions.explain: Azole antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole) are potent CYP inhibitors that block warfarin metabolism, elevating plasma levels and bleeding risk.

open.q: Explain why adding ketoconazole or fluconazole to a patient taking warfarin causes an elevated INR and bleeding.
accept: inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes

questions.q: During paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose, depletion of hepatic glutathione leads to hepatocellular necrosis caused by which toxic reactive intermediate?
questions.explain: When glucuronidation and sulfation pathways are saturated in paracetamol overdose, CYP2E1 oxidizes paracetamol to NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and binds covalently to hepatocyte proteins.

open.q: Name the toxic reactive metabolite responsible for hepatotoxicity in paracetamol overdose.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a drug whose Phase I metabolite is pharmacologically active and prolongs the clinical duration of action?
options: Aspirin converted to salicylic acid, which is immediately inert
Diazepam converted to desmethyldiazepam (nordiazepam) and oxazepam
Penicillin G hydrolyzed to penicilloic acid
questions.explain: Diazepam is metabolized to active benzodiazepines (nordiazepam, temazepam, oxazepam) with long half-lives, accounting for prolonged sedation.

open.q: Name an active metabolite of diazepam that contributes to its prolonged sedative effect.

questions.q: Which three physiological processes in the nephron determine the net renal excretion of a drug?
options: Hepatic extraction, biliary secretion and enterohepatic cycling
Glomerular filtration, tubular secretion and reabsorption
questions.explain: Renal drug excretion = (Glomerular filtration + Tubular secretion) - Tubular reabsorption.

open.q: List the three renal physiological processes that govern the urinary excretion of drugs.
accept: glomerular filtration tubular secretion and tubular reabsorption

questions.q: In which segment of the nephron does active carrier-mediated secretion of organic anions (like penicillins and probenecid) and organic cations (like morphine and cimetidine) occur?
questions.explain: The proximal convoluted tubule expresses OAT (organic anion transporters) and OCT (organic cation transporters) that actively secrete both free and protein-bound drugs into tubular fluid.

open.q: Name the nephron segment where active tubular secretion of organic acids and bases takes place.

questions.q: Why was probenecid historically co-administered with penicillin G during World War II and in single-dose gonorrhoea regimens?
options: Probenecid competes for tubular organic-anion transport, reducing penicillin secretion
It increases intestinal absorption of penicillin
questions.explain: Probenecid is an organic acid that competitively inhibits OAT-mediated tubular secretion of penicillin, raising plasma penicillin levels and extending its duration of action.

open.q: Explain the pharmacokinetic mechanism by which probenecid prolongs the plasma half-life of penicillin.
accept: competitively inhibits active tubular secretion in the proximal tubule
blocks organic anion transporter secretion of penicillin

questions.q: A 24-year-old patient presents to the emergency room following an intentional overdose of aspirin (salicylate). Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is administered as part of management. How does sodium bicarbonate accelerate salicylate elimination?
options: It neutralises aspirin in the stomach
Urine alkalinisation increases salicylate ionisation and reduces reabsorption
It chelates salicylate for biliary excretion
questions.explain: Alkalinizing urine raises tubular fluid pH, shifting weak acids like salicylate and phenobarbital into their ionized (A-) form, trapping them in urine for rapid excretion.

open.q: Explain how intravenous sodium bicarbonate enhances the renal clearance of aspirin (salicylate) in overdose.
accept: urinary alkalinization ionizes salicylate and prevents tubular reabsorption
alkalinizes urine causing ion trapping of weak acid

questions.q: Which intervention can be used to accelerate the renal excretion of a weakly basic drug such as amphetamine or phencyclidine in acute poisoning?
options: Alkalinization of urine with sodium bicarbonate
Acidification of urine with ammonium chloride or ascorbic acid
Administration of intravenous lipid emulsion only
questions.explain: Acidifying the urine protonates weak bases (BH+), increasing their ionized fraction in tubular fluid and reducing passive back-diffusion into peritubular capillaries.

open.q: How does altering urinary pH accelerate the renal elimination of a weakly basic drug overdose?
accept: acidifying the urine ionizes the weak base and prevents tubular reabsorption

questions.q: What is enterohepatic circulation (enterohepatic recycling) and how does it affect a drug's pharmacokinetics?
options: Drugs pass directly from colon to lungs
The stomach secretes drugs into portal blood
Biliary conjugates are deconjugated by gut bacteria and reabsorbed
questions.explain: Drugs like morphine, chloramphenicol, and ethinylestradiol are excreted in bile as glucuronides, cleaved by intestinal flora back to active lipophilic drug, and reabsorbed, extending their duration.

open.q: Describe enterohepatic circulation and state its effect on a drug's plasma half-life.
accept: biliary excretion bacterial deconjugation and intestinal reabsorption prolonging half-life
recirculation between liver bile and intestine extending duration of action

questions.q: How is drug clearance (CL) formally defined in pharmacokinetics?
options: The theoretical volume of plasma completely cleared of a drug per unit time
The total mass of drug excreted in urine over 24 hours
The time required for plasma drug concentration to decrease by 50%
The fraction of an oral dose that escapes first-pass metabolism
questions.explain: Clearance (expressed in mL/min or L/h) is the proportionality constant relating the rate of drug elimination to the plasma drug concentration (CL = Rate of elimination / Cp).

open.q: Define drug clearance (CL).
accept: volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time
rate of elimination divided by plasma concentration

questions.q: Which characteristic defines first-order elimination kinetics, followed by most drugs at therapeutic concentrations?
options: A fixed amount is eliminated per unit time
A fixed fraction is eliminated per unit time
Half-life doubles with each dose increase
questions.explain: In first-order (linear) kinetics, metabolizing enzymes and transporters are unsaturated, so elimination rate is directly proportional to plasma concentration and half-life remains constant.

open.q: State the defining feature of first-order drug elimination kinetics.
accept: constant fraction or percentage eliminated per unit time
rate of elimination is proportional to plasma concentration

questions.q: Which characteristic defines zero-order (saturation) elimination kinetics?
options: A fixed percentage is cleared each hour
A fixed amount is eliminated per unit time when enzymes are saturated
Clearance is unchanged at all doses
questions.explain: In zero-order kinetics, elimination capacity is saturated; a fixed mass of drug is removed per hour, and small dose increments cause disproportionately large spikes in plasma concentration.

open.q: State the defining feature of zero-order drug elimination kinetics.
accept: constant amount of drug eliminated per unit time
saturated elimination independent of plasma concentration

questions.q: Which group of drugs classically exhibits zero-order (capacity-limited) elimination kinetics at therapeutic or modestly elevated concentrations?
questions.explain: Ethanol (alcohol dehydrogenase saturation), phenytoin (CYP2C9/2C19 saturation near therapeutic range), and high-dose aspirin show zero-order kinetics.

open.q: Name three classic drugs that exhibit zero-order elimination kinetics.

questions.q: Which mathematical equation correctly relates elimination half-life (t1/2), apparent volume of distribution (Vd), and total body clearance (CL) for a drug obeying first-order kinetics?
questions.explain: Half-life is directly proportional to the volume of distribution and inversely proportional to clearance: t1/2 = (ln 2 x Vd) / CL = (0.693 x Vd) / CL.

open.q: Write the pharmacokinetic equation relating elimination half-life (t1/2) to volume of distribution (Vd) and clearance (CL).
accept: half-life equals 0.693 times Vd divided by CL

questions.q: A drug has an apparent volume of distribution (Vd) of 40 L and a total body clearance (CL) of 6.93 L/h. What is its elimination half-life (t1/2)?

open.q: Calculate the elimination half-life of a drug with a Vd of 40 L and a clearance of 6.93 L/h.

questions.q: Approximately how many elimination half-lives are required for a drug administered at a constant dosing rate to reach over 95% of its steady-state plasma concentration (Css)?
questions.explain: After 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 half-lives, plasma concentration reaches 50%, 75%, 87.5%, 93.75%, and 96.875% of steady state, respectively; thus 4 to 5 half-lives are needed.

open.q: How many elimination half-lives does it take for a drug to reach steady-state plasma concentration during continuous infusion or repeated fixed dosing?

questions.q: If the maintenance dosing rate of a drug obeying first-order kinetics is doubled, how does the time required to reach the new steady-state concentration change?
options: It is unchanged because steady state depends on half-life
questions.explain: Doubling the dosing rate doubles the steady-state plasma concentration (Css), but the time taken to reach that plateau still equals 4 to 5 elimination half-lives.

open.q: If you double the maintenance infusion rate of a first-order drug, what happens to the steady-state concentration and the time required to reach steady state?
accept: Css doubles while time to steady state stays the same
steady state level doubles and time is unchanged

questions.q: Which pharmacokinetic parameter determines the size of an initial intravenous loading dose required to achieve a target plasma concentration immediately?
questions.explain: Loading dose (LD) = (Target plasma concentration x Vd) / Bioavailability (F). It fills the volume of distribution immediately without waiting 4 to 5 half-lives.

open.q: Which primary pharmacokinetic parameter is used to calculate the loading dose of a drug?

questions.q: Which pharmacokinetic parameter determines the maintenance dosing rate needed to keep plasma drug concentration at a desired steady state?
questions.explain: At steady state, Rate of drug administration = Rate of elimination = CL x Css; thus Maintenance Dose = (CL x Css x dosing interval) / F.

open.q: Which primary pharmacokinetic parameter determines the maintenance dose rate required to sustain a target steady-state concentration?

questions.q: A 65-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is started on digoxin (Vd = 500 L, oral bioavailability = 0.7). To achieve an immediate target plasma concentration of 1.4 mcg/L, what oral loading dose is required?
questions.explain: Loading dose = (Target Cp x Vd) / F = (1.4 mcg/L x 500 L) / 0.7 = 700 / 0.7 = 1000 mcg (1.0 mg).

open.q: Calculate the oral loading dose needed to achieve a target plasma concentration of 1.4 mcg/L for a drug with a Vd of 500 L and oral bioavailability of 0.7.

questions.q: A patient with severe chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance 15 mL/min) requires gentamicin, which is eliminated almost exclusively by glomerular filtration. How should the dosing regimen be adjusted?
options: Give a usual loading dose, then reduce maintenance dose or extend interval
Double both loading and maintenance doses
Switch to oral dosing to increase clearance
questions.explain: Renal failure reduces clearance (CL) and prolongs half-life, while Vd is usually unchanged; therefore a full loading dose is still needed to reach therapeutic levels promptly, followed by a reduced maintenance regimen.

open.q: How should the loading dose and maintenance dose of a renally cleared drug like gentamicin be modified in severe renal failure?
accept: normal loading dose with reduced maintenance dose or extended interval
keep loading dose unchanged and lower maintenance dose

questions.q: After stopping a drug that follows first-order elimination kinetics, approximately what percentage of the drug has been eliminated from the body after 4 half-lives?
questions.explain: Remaining drug is (1/2)^4 = 1/16 = 6.25%, meaning 93.75% has been eliminated after 4 half-lives (and 96.875% after 5 half-lives).

open.q: What percentage of a drug is eliminated from the body after 4 elimination half-lives?

questions.q: What does a high hepatic extraction ratio (E > 0.7), as seen with morphine, propranolol, and verapamil, imply for their hepatic clearance?
options: Hepatic clearance depends entirely on plasma protein binding
Hepatic clearance is unaffected by liver blood flow
Hepatic clearance is flow-limited and depends primarily on hepatic blood flow
Hepatic clearance is zero in healthy adults
questions.explain: For high-extraction drugs, the liver clears almost all drug delivered to it; thus hepatic clearance equals hepatic blood flow (QH) and drops sharply in heart failure or shock.

open.q: For a drug with a high hepatic extraction ratio (such as propranolol or lidocaine), which physiological factor is the rate-limiting determinant of hepatic clearance?

questions.q: For a drug with a low hepatic extraction ratio (E < 0.3) such as warfarin or phenytoin, which two factors primarily govern hepatic clearance?
options: Hepatic arterial pressure and biliary sphincter tone
Intrinsic hepatic clearance and unbound fraction
questions.explain: Low-extraction drugs are capacity-limited; hepatic clearance approximates fu x CLint and is sensitive to CYP enzyme induction/inhibition and changes in plasma protein binding.

open.q: Name the two main determinants of hepatic clearance for a low-extraction drug such as warfarin.
accept: intrinsic enzyme activity and unbound drug fraction
CYP metabolic capacity and free fraction

questions.q: Why is therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) routinely performed for drugs such as digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, gentamicin, and vancomycin?
options: They have narrow therapeutic indices and variable kinetics
They are non-toxic at any concentration
All have half-lives under five minutes
questions.explain: TDM guides dosing when the margin between minimum effective concentration and minimum toxic concentration is narrow and pharmacokinetics vary widely across patients.

open.q: State two key pharmacokinetic or clinical criteria that justify therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) for a medication.
accept: narrow therapeutic index and wide inter-individual pharmacokinetic variability
narrow therapeutic window and unpredictable plasma levels

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a non-microsomal Phase I enzyme located in the cytoplasm or plasma rather than the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
questions.explain: Esterases (such as plasma cholinesterase hydrolyzing succinylcholine and procaine), alcohol dehydrogenase, and monoamine oxidase are non-microsomal enzymes.

open.q: Give an example of a non-microsomal enzyme involved in drug metabolism.

questions.q: A 32-year-old surgical patient receives intravenous succinylcholine for rapid-sequence endotracheal intubation and remains paralysed and apnoeic for 4 hours instead of the usual 5 to 10 minutes. Which pharmacogenetic abnormality explains this prolonged paralysis?
questions.explain: Succinylcholine is normally hydrolyzed within minutes by plasma butyrylcholinesterase; patients with an inherited atypical variant experience prolonged neuromuscular blockade ('scoline apnoea').

open.q: Name the plasma enzyme whose genetic deficiency causes prolonged paralysis (scoline apnoea) after succinylcholine administration.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes Hofmann elimination, the mechanism by which atracurium is cleared from the body?
options: Spontaneous non-enzymatic breakdown at physiological pH
questions.explain: Hofmann elimination is spontaneous temperature- and pH-dependent molecular cleavage independent of liver or kidney function, making atracurium safe in hepatic and renal failure.

open.q: Define Hofmann elimination and name a neuromuscular blocker cleared by this mechanism.
accept: spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation at physiological pH and temperature seen with atracurium
pH and temperature dependent spontaneous breakdown of atracurium

questions.q: How does extensive hypoalbuminaemia (as seen in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis) affect a highly albumin-bound drug like phenytoin?
options: The unbound fraction rises, increasing toxicity despite a normal total level
The free fraction falls to zero
questions.explain: Low serum albumin leaves a higher proportion of phenytoin unbound; total measured drug may look normal or low while free active drug is in the toxic range.

open.q: Explain why a patient with severe hypoalbuminaemia can develop phenytoin toxicity despite a normal total plasma phenytoin level.
accept: increased unbound free fraction of phenytoin
higher free active drug concentration due to reduced protein binding

questions.q: Why does phenytoin exhibit a sudden, steep rise in plasma concentration when its daily dose is increased slightly near the upper end of its therapeutic range?
options: Enzyme saturation shifts elimination toward zero-order kinetics
questions.explain: Phenytoin displays Michaelis-Menten (non-linear) kinetics: once hepatic enzymes approach saturation (Km), clearance falls and small dose increases cause disproportionate jumps in plasma levels.

open.q: Explain why small increases in the maintenance dose of phenytoin can cause unexpectedly large increases in plasma concentration and toxicity.
accept: saturation of hepatic metabolizing enzymes shifting to zero-order kinetics

questions.q: Besides the kidneys and hepatobiliary system, which route is the primary pathway for eliminating volatile general anesthetics such as halothane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane?
questions.explain: Volatile and gaseous anesthetics diffuse down a partial-pressure gradient from pulmonary capillary blood into alveolar gas and are eliminated unchanged via exhalation.

open.q: Name the principal organ responsible for eliminating volatile general anesthetics from the body.
